quiz.title: Half-Angle Identities & Trig Integration Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on rewriting 1 ± cos x with half-angle identities, integrating powers of cosec and cot, and finishing a definite trig integral. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Exemplar Class 12 integration Q41 — half-angle simplification and definite trig integrals

questions.q: Which identity rewrites 1 + cos x for this problem?
questions.explanation: From cos x = 2 cos²(x/2) − 1, adding 1 to both sides gives 1 + cos x = 2 cos²(x/2).
Since cos x = 1 − 2 sin²(x/2), subtracting from 1 gives 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2).

questions.q: Using the two identities, (1 + cos x)/(1 − cos x) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: The ratio is 2 cos²(x/2) over 2 sin²(x/2) = cos²(x/2)/sin²(x/2) = cot²(x/2).

questions.q: Therefore √[(1 + cos x)/(1 − cos x)] equals:
questions.explanation: The square root of cot²(x/2) is |cot(x/2)|; the modulus matters because sign depends on the interval of x.
Since d/dx(cot x) = −cosec² x, we get ∫ cosec² x dx = −cot x + C.
The derivative of cot x is −cosec² x, the identity that makes cot terms easy to integrate.

questions.q: What is ∫ cosec x cot x dx?
questions.explanation: Since d/dx(cosec x) = −cosec x cot x, the integral is −cosec x + C.

questions.q: On the interval [π, 3π/2], x/2 lies in [π/2, 3π/4], where cot(x/2) is:
questions.explanation: For x/2 in the second quadrant [π/2, 3π/4], cosine is negative and sine positive, so cot(x/2) = cos/sin is negative. This sign controls how |cot(x/2)| is unwrapped before integrating.

faq.q: Why do we use half-angle identities on this integral?
faq.a: The integrand mixes 1 + cos x and 1 − cos x, which resist standard formulas. Rewriting them as 2 cos²(x/2) and 2 sin²(x/2) collapses the ratio into a single power of cot(x/2), turning the problem into an integral of cosec and cot terms you already know.

faq.q: Why does the modulus appear when taking the square root?
faq.a: √(cot²(x/2)) is |cot(x/2)|, not cot(x/2). On the limits π to 3π/2 the angle x/2 sits in the second quadrant, where cot is negative, so |cot(x/2)| = −cot(x/2). Dropping the modulus is the most common way students lose marks here.

faq.q: Which integration formulas do I actually need?
faq.a: Just three: ∫ cosec² x dx = −cot x + C, ∫ cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C, and ∫ cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x| + C. After the half-angle simplification the whole problem reduces to these standard results.

faq.q: Do the limits change when I switch to x/2?
faq.a: If you substitute u = x/2 then yes — the limits become u = π/2 to u = 3π/4, and dx = 2 du. Many students keep x as the variable and simply evaluate the antiderivative at π and 3π/2, which is fine as long as the modulus sign is handled first.
